Commodity-backed (gold, or silver, or whatever you want it to be) currency, but operating entirely within the free market. Most likely not done with physical gold, but banks would issue notes that are freely redeemable for X ounces of gold. Most likely each major bank would have its own form of currency, but market pressures will create a pretty strong incentive for the value to be standardized--One Bank A dollar would trade for the same amount of gold as Bank B's dollar--so you'd have mixed currencies in circulation. Due again to market pressures, Bank A would freely take deposits of cash denoted in Bank B's dollars--they'd be a lot less consumer-friendly if they didn't do this, and Bank A could always trade the B-dollars it has to the A-dollars that Bank A has without any real drawbacks, and vice-versa. Most likely you'd only be get gold for A-dollars at Bank A, however. There's precedence for this back when Europe was mostly gold and silver coins--merchants that did a lot of international trading would be pretty happy to take payment in multiple country's currency as long as the gold value was the same.

Now, the one concern people usually have with a system like this is that it's still possible for a very wealthy man (or group of people) to manipulate the economy by buying or selling vast amounts of gold. However, the dangers of this are somewhat overstated. For one, it's somewhat self-correcting--if one entity sells a large quantity of gold and floods the economy with it, the sudden lower price of gold means a whole bunch of other actors are now much more willing to buy it. This makes the price go back up to where it was before as people buy the gold and the supply of it in the market is reduced, so besides the extremely short run there isn't a drawback to the economy. This also touches upon game theory--there won't be very many people in the world that have the wealth to do this, so any attempt by one man to influence the economy a certain way will be countered by a different man wishing to influence the economy another way. These people could try and cooperate and form a "gold cartel", in which they collude and agree not to act against each other's interests, but both game/economic theory and historical data proves that cartels, or any similar conspiracy, isn't economically stable. The moment any one member of the cartel realizes his own personal gain is being held back by the less competent members of the cartel he'll break the collusion agreement for his own gain (the Prisoner's Dilemma is a good, simplified example of this if you read into it more), and the cartel is broken. Furthermore, all of this is based on the assumption that gold is the only commodity that's backing trade, but in a free market, it wouldn't be. Some banks would use gold, some would use silver, a few limited areas might use oil (oil doesn't really work as a currency on the micro scale because it's rather annoying to transport by hand, but you might see it in limited quantities at the macro level), and a lot of banks would use a basket of commodites; they would denote their money in gold, AND in silver, AND in copper, or whatever other commodity they feel is best for them. This would allow them to fall back their alternatives if there was some kind of shock to the market of one material or the other. So if the price of say, gold was fluctuating rapidly because some new giant-ass mine was just discovered, or a company brought some over from an asteroid, they could temporarily not to any business in gold until the price settles down, and fall back on their backup commodities instead.
